games.explanation: The market is looking at Baltimore as a coin flip when they're actually the meaningfully better team on paper, and a near-pick'em on the road dog is where that pricing gets interesting. Alonso and Henderson are the kind of right-handed bats that don't care much about Brandon Young's warts, and the Orioles get to attack with a lineup whose top four all post xwOBAs against righties north of .320. Philadelphia counters with Schwarber and Harper, which is real, but Turner sits at a pedestrian .320 xwOBA and the middle of that order thins out fast. At -114 you're getting the better roster at a price that treats this like a 52% game, and our number says it's closer to 59%.

Cleveland is the shorter price here mostly on reputation, because Tanner Bibee is a fine pitcher who happens to be walking into the wrong lineup. Arizona's top four all hit right-handed pitching hard, and Bibee's contact profile against righties (a 38% hard-hit rate and a barrel problem he hasn't solved all year) is exactly what Carroll and Marte feast on. Cleveland's counter is Jose Ramirez and a lot of hoping, with Angel Martinez and a sub-.260 xwOBA leading things off. When the better team is also the better matchup and you're getting plus money, the ticket writes itself. +115 on the road dog with the lineup edge is the whole story.

Bryce Miller is being priced like the Mariners' rotation still has its early-season shine, but the underlying numbers say he's a hittable righty who happens to be facing the better team on the field. Zebby Matthews misses more bats and walks fewer hitters, and Josh Bell in particular has been feasting on right-handed pitching to the tune of a .384 xwOBA. The park keeps the roof closed and the run environment down, which is exactly the kind of low-scoring coin flip where the underdog cashes more than the market wants to admit. Getting +158 on the club our sim treats as a near even-money favorite is the entire argument.

Detroit is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but the market is pricing this like a coronation when the sim spits out a one-run game. Casey Mize gets barreled up more than his ERA suggests, and an Athletics lineup that runs Soderstrom and Langeliers into a hittable righty is not the pushover the number implies. Springs quietly matches Mize in xwOBA-against, which turns this into the kind of grinding four-to-five run affair where a run and a half is an enormous cushion. Our number says the Athletics cover better than 63% of the time, and the board is giving you a coin flip. Take the points and the plus juice.
